The emitted photon's energy equals the level difference, not the level's absolute energy.
learning_objectives: Explain why atomic spectra are discrete rather than continuous.
Relate the photon frequency to the energy difference between two levels.
real_world_applications: Lasers exploit population differences between quantized energy levels.
Atomic clocks rely on precise transitions between energy levels.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Radioactivity
entities.definition: The spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable atomic nucleus. The three main types are alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays.
examples: Carbon-14 dating is used on ancient organic remains; radioactive tracers image organs in medicine.
Smoke detectors contain a small alpha-emitting source.
key_experiments: Use a Geiger counter to detect background radiation and compare shielding/absorption of different sources.
Detecting radiation using a Geiger-Muller tube.
common_misconceptions: Radioactivity is always man-made (it occurs naturally).
All radiation is harmful (we are exposed to natural background radiation daily).
Radioactive materials glow (they are invisible; only their effects can be detected).
learning_objectives: Describe radioactivity as spontaneous nuclear decay.
Distinguish between alpha, beta, and gamma radiation.
Explain half-life and calculate remaining amounts.
Describe uses and hazards of radiation.

entities.name: Ray Model of Light
entities.definition: A simplified geometric model of light propagation in which light is represented as straight lines (rays) traveling through transparent media and changing direction at boundaries via reflection or refraction.
examples: Predicting where a shadow falls using straight light rays.
Designing a simple periscope from plane mirrors.
key_experiments: Shadow-size and pinhole-image experiments with a bright bulb and a card.
common_misconceptions: Light rays are physical objects (light rays are idealized geometric constructs showing direction of energy travel).
Light only travels straight when observed (light travels straight in homogeneous media regardless of observation).
learning_objectives: Construct ray diagrams showing reflection and refraction.
Apply the ray model to explain shadow formation and pinhole cameras.
Explain the limitations of the ray model (e.g. wave phenomena like diffraction).
real_world_applications: Camera lens design and optical instrument engineering.
Eyeglass and contact lens prescription design.

provenance.source: IUPAP / UNESCO Physics Education Standards

entities.name: Reflection of Light
entities.definition: The bouncing back of light from a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
examples: Your image in a plane mirror; sunlight glinting off a lake.
Retroreflectors on bicycles return light to its source.
key_experiments: Ray box at a plane mirror: measure and show angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
Verifying the law of reflection using a plane mirror and ray box.
common_misconceptions: Reflection only happens from mirrors (all surfaces reflect some light).
The angle of incidence is measured from the surface (it is measured from the normal).
Rough surfaces do not reflect (they reflect diffusely).
learning_objectives: State the law of reflection.
Draw ray diagrams for reflection from plane mirrors.
Distinguish between regular and diffuse reflection.
Explain how images are formed in plane mirrors.

entities.name: Refraction of Light
entities.definition: The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in light's speed in different media.
entities.equation: n = c/v (refractive index) ; Snell's law: n₁·sin(θ₁) = n₂·sin(θ₂)
examples: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent.
A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
key_experiments: Ray box through a rectangular glass block: trace the rays, measure angles, and verify Snell's law.
Bending of light through a glass block.
Apparent depth of a coin in water.
common_misconceptions: Light bends because it changes direction randomly (bending is systematic and governed by Snell's law).
Refraction only happens with glass (it happens at any boundary between different media).
Refraction changes the color of light (dispersion does, not refraction itself).
learning_objectives: Define refraction and explain why light bends.
Use Snell's law to calculate angles of refraction.
Explain apparent depth and other everyday refraction effects.
Describe total internal reflection and its applications.

entities.name: Electrical Resistance
entities.definition: The opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor. Resistance converts electrical energy to thermal energy.
examples: A thin wire resists more than a thick one; metal conducts far better than wood.
Heater elements are deliberately high-resistance so they heat up.
key_experiments: Vary the voltage across a fixed resistor and plot current against voltage — straight line at constant temperature.
common_misconceptions: Resistance is the same as voltage (resistance is opposition; voltage is potential difference).
Thicker wires always have less resistance (all else equal, yes — but length and material also matter).
Resistance is always undesirable (resistance enables heating, lighting, and control).
learning_objectives: Define resistance as opposition to current.
Calculate resistance from voltage and current.
Explain factors affecting resistance (material, length, cross-sectional area, temperature).
Use the resistance formula R = ρL/A.

entities.name: Scalar Quantity
entities.definition: A quantity that has magnitude but no direction. Scalars are fully described by a numerical value and a unit, and follow ordinary arithmetic rules of addition.
examples: Temperature 30 °C, speed 50 km/h and mass 5 kg are scalars — no direction.
Energy and time are scalars.
key_experiments: Sort a list of physical quantities into scalars and vectors.
common_misconceptions: Scalars are less important than vectors (both are essential; many key quantities are scalars).
All numbers in physics are scalars (quantities like velocity have both magnitude and direction).
learning_objectives: Distinguish scalars from vectors.
Identify common scalar quantities in physics.
Perform arithmetic with scalar quantities correctly.

entities.name: Simple Harmonic Motion
entities.definition: Motion in which the restoring force on an object is directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction, producing a sinusoidal variation of displacement with time.
examples: A mass on an ideal spring oscillating about its equilibrium position.
A pendulum swinging through small angles approximates simple harmonic motion.
key_experiments: Hang a mass on a spring, displace it, and log its position to reveal sinusoidal motion.
common_misconceptions: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is greatest at the extremes where the speed is zero, not at equilibrium.
The period of a simple pendulum is independent of the amplitude only for small angles, not universally.
learning_objectives: Describe the condition under which motion qualifies as simple harmonic.
Relate displacement, velocity, and acceleration across the oscillation cycle.
real_world_applications: Suspension and shock-absorber design on vehicles.
Mechanical clocks and tuning-fork timing references.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Sound
entities.definition: A mechanical wave produced by vibrating objects, transmitted through a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) as a longitudinal wave. Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
examples: An echo returns from a cliff; SONAR measures depth by reflected sound.
A siren sounds higher pitched as it approaches (Doppler effect).
key_experiments: Electric bell in a vacuum jar: the sound fades as air is pumped out — sound needs a medium.
Tuning fork in water (vibrations create waves).
Bell jar experiment (sound needs a medium).
common_misconceptions: Sound can travel through space (sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through vacuum).
Sound travels faster than light (sound is much slower: ~343 m/s vs. 3×10⁸ m/s).
Sound always travels at the same speed (speed varies with medium and temperature).
learning_objectives: Explain that sound is produced by vibrations.
Describe how sound travels through different media.
Explain why sound cannot travel through vacuum.
Relate loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency.

entities.name: Specific Heat Capacity
entities.definition: The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 kelvin (or 1 degree Celsius). Different substances have different specific heat capacities.
examples: Water heats and cools slowly — its high specific heat (~4200 J/kg·°C) moderates coastal climates.
Sand on a beach warms faster than the sea in sunshine.
key_experiments: Electric-heater method: measure electrical energy in (P·t), the temperature rise, and compute c = Q/(m·ΔT).
Calorimetry experiment to measure specific heat of a metal.
common_misconceptions: Specific heat is the same for all substances (it varies significantly — water has very high specific heat).
Higher specific heat means the object is hotter (specific heat is about how much energy is needed to change temperature, not the temperature itself).
Specific heat depends on mass (it is a property of the substance, independent of mass).
learning_objectives: Define specific heat capacity.
Calculate heat transfer using Q = mcΔT.
Explain why water is effective as a coolant.
Compare specific heats of different substances.
real_world_applications: Car radiators (water's high specific heat absorbs engine heat).
Cooking utensils (metals with low specific heat heat quickly).

entities.name: Speed
entities.definition: The rate at which an object covers distance — the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken. Speed is a scalar quantity.
examples: A car speedometer reads 60 km/h.
A marathon runner's average speed over the whole race.
key_experiments: Time a measured distance with a stopwatch and compute average speed.
Measuring the speed of a moving object using a stopwatch and ruler.
common_misconceptions: Speed and velocity are always the same (velocity includes direction; speed does not).
Speed is always constant (speed can change continuously).
Average speed is the average of speeds (it is total distance divided by total time).
learning_objectives: Calculate speed from distance and time.
Distinguish between speed and velocity.
Calculate average speed for multi-segment journeys.
Interpret speed from distance-time graphs.

entities.name: Temperature
entities.definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Temperature determines the direction of heat flow — heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
examples: A clinical thermometer reads 37 °C body temperature; a room thermostat is set near 20 °C.
Melting ice stays at 0 °C even while it absorbs heat.
key_experiments: Calibrate a thermometer at the ice point and the steam point.
common_misconceptions: Temperature measures heat (temperature measures average kinetic energy; heat is energy transfer).
Temperature depends on the size of the object (temperature is independent of mass — a small hot object can have higher temperature than a large cold one).
Absolute zero is the temperature at which all motion stops (quantum mechanics prevents complete stop, but it is the theoretical minimum).
learning_objectives: Define temperature as a measure of average kinetic energy.
Convert between Celsius and Kelvin scales.
Explain why heat flows from hot to cold.
Use thermometers to measure temperature accurately.

entities.name: Thermal Energy
entities.definition: The total internal kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a substance, associated with their random motion and interactions. Thermal energy is related to temperature but distinct from it — it depends on mass, temperature, and the nature of the substance.
examples: Rubbing your hands converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.
Thermal energy from the Sun warms Earth's surface.
key_experiments: Compare how fast identical cans of hot water cool when wrapped in different insulators.
common_misconceptions: Thermal energy and temperature are the same (temperature is average kinetic energy per particle; thermal energy includes all particles).
Thermal energy is only in hot objects (all objects have thermal energy).
Thermal energy can be completely converted to work (second law limits conversion).
learning_objectives: Define thermal energy as the internal energy of a substance.
Distinguish between thermal energy, heat, and temperature.
Explain how thermal energy changes during heating and cooling.
Analyze thermal energy transfer in everyday situations.

entities.name: Time
entities.definition: The dimension that orders events from past through present to future, measured as the interval between two events. Time is a scalar quantity and one of the fundamental base quantities in physics.
key_experiments: Time repeated pendulum swings and average to measure the period with small error.
examples: Timing a 100 m sprint with a stopwatch.
The time for one complete pendulum swing is its period.
common_misconceptions: Time is the same as a clock reading (time is the dimension; clocks measure intervals of it).
Time passes at the same rate for all observers (at relativistic speeds, time dilation occurs).
learning_objectives: Define time as a fundamental physical quantity.
Measure time intervals using appropriate instruments.
Use time as the independent variable in motion analysis.

entities.name: Unit of Measurement
entities.definition: A standard reference amount of a physical quantity, defined and adopted by convention, against which measurements of that quantity are compared. Units provide the scale that gives physical meaning to numerical values.
examples: The second (s), metre (m) and kilogram (kg) are SI base units.
SI prefixes: kilo-, centi-, milli- and micro- scale the base units.
key_experiments: Unit-conversion practice: convert between mm, cm, m, km and ms, s for measured lengths and times.
common_misconceptions: Units are part of the object being measured (units are conventions, not properties of objects).
Any number can have any unit (units must match the quantity being measured).
learning_objectives: Explain why standardized units are necessary.
Convert between common units for a given quantity.
Identify the SI base units for fundamental quantities.
real_world_applications: International trade (standardized mass and volume units).
Scientific reproducibility (any lab can replicate using SI units).

entities.name: Vector Quantity
entities.definition: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, and follows specific rules of addition (vector addition). Vectors represent quantities where direction matters as much as size.
examples: Force '10 N north' and wind '40 km/h north-east' are vectors.
Displacement arrows drawn on a map.
key_experiments: Walk 3 m east then 4 m north: a 5 m resultant (3-4-5 triangle) demonstrates vector addition.
common_misconceptions: Any quantity with direction is a vector (must also follow vector addition rules).
Vectors are just arrows on paper (they represent physical quantities with real effects).
learning_objectives: Distinguish vectors from scalars.
Represent vectors graphically.
Add vectors using the triangle or parallelogram method.
real_world_applications: Navigation (wind velocity + aircraft velocity = ground velocity).
Engineering forces (multiple forces on a structure).
Physics of motion (velocity, acceleration, force are all vectors).

entities.name: Velocity
entities.definition: The rate of change of displacement with respect to time. Velocity is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude (speed) and direction.
examples: A plane flying 800 km/h due west — speed plus direction.
A car's velocity changes when it turns, even if speed is constant.
key_experiments: Motion sensor tracking a walk: velocity shows negative values when the walker reverses direction.
Motion sensor experiments plotting position vs. time to extract velocity.
common_misconceptions: Velocity is just speed with a direction (the vector nature has real mathematical consequences).
Higher speed always means higher velocity (if directions differ, they are different velocities).
Velocity must be constant to be defined (instantaneous velocity exists at every point).
learning_objectives: Define velocity as a vector quantity.
Calculate velocity from displacement and time.
Distinguish between average and instantaneous velocity.
Interpret velocity from position-time graphs (slope).

entities.name: Potential Difference (Voltage)
entities.definition: The work done per unit charge to move a charge between two points in an electric circuit. Voltage is the "push" that drives current through a circuit.
examples: A 9 V battery provides 9 V of potential difference across a circuit; household mains is roughly 230 V.
Voltage is the 'push' that drives charge around a circuit.
key_experiments: Measure the terminal voltage of a battery with a voltmeter at no load and under load.
common_misconceptions: Voltage and current are the same (voltage is potential difference; current is flow).
A battery creates current (a battery provides voltage; current depends on resistance).
Voltage is "used up" in a circuit (voltage drops across components, but energy is conserved).
learning_objectives: Define potential difference as work done per unit charge.
Calculate voltage from work and charge.
Measure voltage using a voltmeter.
Explain why voltage drives current.
real_world_applications: Electrical outlets (120V or 230V depending on country).

entities.name: Wave
entities.definition: A disturbance that transfers energy through a medium or through space, without permanently displacing the medium. Waves transfer energy and information from one place to another.
examples: Sound travels through air as a longitudinal wave.
Light and radio travel as transverse electromagnetic waves and need no medium.
key_experiments: Slinky: a sideways flick makes a transverse pulse; a push-pull makes a longitudinal pulse.
Ripple tank experiments demonstrating reflection, refraction, and diffraction of water waves.
common_misconceptions: Waves carry matter (waves carry energy; the medium oscillates but does not travel with the wave).
All waves need a medium (electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum).
Waves always move in straight lines (waves can diffract and refract).
learning_objectives: Define wave as a disturbance that transfers energy.
Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Identify wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed on a wave diagram.
Relate wave speed, frequency, and wavelength using v = f·λ.

entities.name: Wave Interference
entities.definition: The superposition of two or more waves at a point resulting in a combined disturbance whose amplitude is the sum of the individual amplitudes. Constructive interference occurs when waves are in phase and destructive interference when they are out of phase.
entities.equation: A_result = A1 + A2 (in phase); A_result = |A1 - A2| (oppositely phased)
examples: Two loudspeakers driven in phase create alternating loud and quiet regions in a room.
Two coherent light sources produce alternating bright and dark interference fringes.
key_experiments: Young's double-slit experiment demonstrates interference fringes from coherent light.
The ripple tank shows constructive and destructive interference of surface waves.
common_misconceptions: Interference does not require the waves to be alike; it is a linear superposition effect.
Destructive interference destroys energy; it redistributes it spatially instead.
learning_objectives: Predict whether two waves add constructively or destructively from their phase difference.
Explain how coherent sources are required for stable observed interference patterns.
real_world_applications: Anti-reflection coatings on optical lenses use destructive thin-film interference.
Interferometry in astronomy and precision length measurement.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics

entities.name: Wave Speed
entities.definition: The speed at which a wave propagates through a medium. Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium, not on frequency or amplitude.
examples: Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air; light at 3×10⁸ m/s.
Deep-ocean tsunami waves can travel at hundreds of km/h.
key_experiments: Ripple tank: measure frequency and wavelength and verify v = f·λ.
common_misconceptions: Higher frequency waves always travel faster (in the same medium, all waves of the same type travel at the same speed).
Wave speed is infinite (all waves have finite speed — light travels at 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum).
learning_objectives: Calculate wave speed from frequency and wavelength.
Explain why wave speed depends on the medium.
Compare wave speeds in different media.
real_world_applications: Thunder and lightning (light travels much faster than sound).

entities.name: Wavelength
entities.definition: The distance between two consecutive points in phase on a wave — for example, crest to crest or trough to trough. Wavelength determines the character of the wave (color of light, pitch of sound).
real_world_applications: The colour of light corresponds to its wavelength.
Antennas are sized to the wavelength they carry; X-ray wavelengths image bones.
examples: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.
Longer radio waves bend around hills more easily than short ones.
key_experiments: Ripple tank: measure the wavelength of periodic waves and change the wave generator frequency.
common_misconceptions: Wavelength is the height of a wave (height is amplitude; wavelength is distance between cycles).
All waves have the same wavelength (wavelength varies enormously — from kilometers to nanometers).
learning_objectives: Define wavelength and identify it on a wave diagram.
Relate wavelength to frequency and wave speed.
Compare wavelengths of different types of waves.

entities.name: Weight
entities.definition: The gravitational force exerted on an object by a massive body (typically Earth). Weight is a vector quantity acting toward the center of the gravitating body.
examples: A 1 kg mass weighs about 9.8 N on Earth but only about 1.6 N on the Moon.
A spring balance reads weight; a beam balance reads mass.
key_experiments: Measure weight with a spring balance and mass with a beam balance for the same object and compare number values.
common_misconceptions: Weight and mass are the same thing (mass is intrinsic; weight is a force that varies with gravity).
Weight is measured in kilograms (kilograms measure mass; newtons measure weight).
An object in free fall is weightless (weight still acts; apparent weight is zero).
learning_objectives: Distinguish between mass and weight.
Calculate weight from mass and gravitational acceleration.
Explain why weight changes with location (different planets, altitudes).
Distinguish between actual weight and apparent weight.
real_world_applications: Weighing scales (measure normal force, which approximates weight on level ground).
Engineering loads (structural design must account for weight).
Athletics (high jump records at high altitude where g is slightly less).

entities.name: Work
entities.definition: Energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement. For a constant force, work equals the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force: W = F·d·cos(θ). Work is a scalar quantity measured in joules.
examples: Lifting a book from the floor to a shelf does positive work on the book.
Holding a heavy weight stationary does no work (no displacement).
Friction does negative work on a sliding block.
common_misconceptions: Work is done whenever a force is applied (work requires displacement in the force direction).
Holding an object stationary requires work (no displacement = no work, despite muscular effort).
Work is a vector quantity (work is scalar; force and displacement are vectors).
learning_objectives: Define work as energy transfer via force through displacement.
Calculate work done by constant and variable forces.
Distinguish positive, negative, and zero work.
Apply the work-energy theorem (W = ΔK).
real_world_applications: Vehicle engines (work done by combustion forces).
Electrical circuits (work done by electric fields on charges).
key_experiments: Measuring work done lifting masses with a force sensor and displacement sensor.
Investigating work done by friction on a sliding block.
Verifying the work-energy theorem with a dynamics cart on a track.

provenance.source: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, 12th Ed.

entities.name: Work-Energy Theorem
entities.definition: The net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. This theorem connects the concept of work (force × distance) directly to the concept of energy.
examples: Braking a car — friction does negative work, removing its kinetic energy.
A hammer driving a nail: the work done transfers kinetic energy into the wood.
key_experiments: Ramp-and-block: the work done pushing a block equals the kinetic energy it gains, within measurement error.
common_misconceptions: Work and kinetic energy are the same thing (work is the process of transferring energy; kinetic energy is the quantity).
Work-energy theorem only applies to constant forces (it applies to any force, constant or varying).
Work done by friction increases kinetic energy (friction does negative work, decreasing kinetic energy).
learning_objectives: State the work-energy theorem.

historical.note: The work-energy theorem is a derived reformulation of Newtonian mechanics rather than a single distinct discovery; it emerges from Newton's laws of motion (1687). Its explicit statement as 'net work equals change in kinetic energy' was consolidated later in the development of energy concepts (18th–19th century).
